title: ITIL fundamentals: incident, problem and change
monthTitle: The Helpdesk Professional: ITIL, Ticketing & Soft Skills
summary: Get a clear, practical grounding in ITIL 4 and the three practices a helpdesk lives by every day: incident, problem, and change management.
objectives: Explain what ITIL is and why organisations adopt it
Define a service, value, and the four dimensions in plain terms
Distinguish an incident from a problem with confidence
Describe the goal of change management and why it protects users
Recognise service requests as distinct from incidents
Apply the correct ITIL practice to a real support scenario

quiz.q: What is the best plain-English definition of an incident in ITIL?
options: A planned upgrade to a system
An unplanned interruption or reduction in quality of a service
quiz.why: An incident is an unplanned event that breaks or degrades a service; the goal of incident management is to restore normal service as fast as possible.

quiz.q: How does a problem differ from an incident?
options: A problem is the underlying cause of one or more incidents
A problem is always less urgent than an incident
quiz.why: Incidents are the visible symptoms; a problem is the root cause behind them. Problem management seeks to remove that cause so incidents stop recurring.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of change management (change enablement)?
options: To stop all changes from happening
To make changes safely while minimising risk and disruption
quiz.why: Change enablement aims to maximise successful changes by assessing and controlling risk, so improvements happen without breaking services for users.

quiz.q: A user asks to be given access to a shared mailbox. Which practice is this?
quiz.why: Nothing is broken — the user wants something provided as a standard offering, which is a service request, handled through request fulfilment, not incident management.

quiz.q: In one sentence, explain the relationship between incidents and problems using an example.
quiz.answer: If five users separately report the same email outage (five incidents), the single failed mail server behind them is the problem, and fixing the server resolves the root cause.
quiz.why: Many incidents can share one underlying problem; problem management removes the cause so the incidents stop happening.

quiz.q: Why does ITIL insist that most changes go through a controlled process?
quiz.answer: Because uncontrolled changes are a leading cause of outages, a controlled process assesses risk and schedules changes so improvements don't break live services.
quiz.why: Change enablement balances the need to improve with the need to protect stable, working services for users.

body_markdown:
## What ITIL is and why it exists

**ITIL** (the IT Infrastructure Library) is the world's most widely adopted framework of **best practices** for IT service management. It is not a rulebook you must obey to the letter — it is a shared vocabulary and set of sensible practices so that IT teams everywhere work in a consistent, reliable way. The current version is **ITIL 4**.

The central idea is **value**: IT exists to help the business and its users achieve outcomes. A **service** is a way of delivering that value — email, the VPN, the finance system are all services. Your job on the desk is to keep those services flowing.

## The three practices you live by

ITIL 4 has many practices, but a helpdesk technician works with three constantly: **incident management**, **problem management**, and **change enablement**. Get these three clear and most of the framework falls into place.

## Incidents: restore service fast

An **incident** is an **unplanned interruption** to a service, or a reduction in its quality. The phone rings, email is down, a laptop won't boot — those are incidents. The single goal of **incident management** is to **restore normal service as quickly as possible**, even with a temporary fix or **workaround**. You are not required to find the deep cause; you are required to get the user working again.

```text
Incident: "Email is down for the whole Sales floor."
Goal: get Sales back on email ASAP, even via a workaround.
```

## Problems: remove the cause

A **problem** is the **underlying cause** of one or more incidents. If twelve people report the same outage, that is twelve incidents and likely one problem. **Problem management** investigates the root cause so the incidents stop coming back. It is slower, more analytical work — often done by Tier 2 and Tier 3.

```text
12 incidents: "Email down" reported by 12 users
 1 problem:   the failed mail server behind all of them
```

Incidents are the *symptoms*; the problem is the *disease*.

## Changes: improve without breaking things

A **change** is the addition, modification, or removal of anything that could affect services — a server patch, a firewall rule, a new application. **Change enablement** exists to make changes **safely**, because uncontrolled changes are one of the biggest causes of outages. Changes are usually assessed for risk and scheduled, sometimes through a **Change Advisory Board (CAB)**. Low-risk, routine changes may be pre-approved as **standard changes**.

## Service requests: nothing is broken

Not every contact is an incident. When a user wants something provided as a normal offering — software installed, access to a mailbox, a new monitor — that is a **service request**, handled through **request fulfilment**. The test is simple: *is something broken, or does the user want something provided?* Broken means incident; provide means request.

## Your task

For each of the following, label it Incident, Problem, Change, or Service Request, and write one sentence justifying your choice:

1. "My screen is frozen and I have a deadline."
2. "Please give me the Adobe Acrobat licence."
3. The network team plans to replace the core switch on Saturday night.
4. The desk has logged 30 tickets this week all about the VPN dropping; someone needs to find out why.

slides.narration: Welcome back. This lesson gives you the framework that quietly shapes almost every professional service desk in the world: ITIL. We'll keep it practical. You'll learn what ITIL is, and then the three practices you'll live by every single day, which are incident, problem, and change management. Get these three clear, and you'll speak the same language as IT professionals everywhere.

slides.title: Services and value
bullets: A service delivers value to users.

Everything else supports that goal.
slides.narration: Two words anchor everything in ITIL: service and value. A service is a way of delivering value, so email, the V P N, and the finance system are all services. When they work, people get their jobs done. Your role on the desk is, very simply, to keep those services flowing for the people who depend on them. Hold onto that idea, because every practice we discuss is ultimately in service of it.

A change is adding, modifying, or removing anything that could affect a service, like a server patch, a firewall rule, or a new app. Change enablement exists to make those changes safely, because uncontrolled changes are one of the biggest causes of outages. Bigger changes get assessed for risk and scheduled, sometimes by a Change Advisory Board. Routine, low-risk ones can be pre-approved as standard changes.

slides.title: Service requests
bullets: The user wants something provided, not fixed.
Software, access, a new monitor.
Handled through request fulfilment.
Test: is it broken, or is it wanted?
slides.narration: Now a crucial distinction. Not every contact is an incident. When a user wants something provided as a normal offering, like software installed, access to a mailbox, or a new monitor, that's a service request, handled through request fulfilment. The simple test is this: is something broken, or does the user just want something provided? If it's broken, it's an incident. If they want something delivered, it's a service request. That single question saves a lot of misrouted tickets.

slides.title: Putting it together
bullets: Incident: restore the broken service.
Problem: remove the recurring cause.
Change: improve without breaking things.
Request: provide a standard offering.
slides.narration: Let's put the four side by side. Incident management restores a broken service fast. Problem management removes the recurring cause so it stops happening. Change enablement lets the team improve and patch things without breaking what already works. And request fulfilment provides standard offerings users ask for. Once you can sort any contact into one of those four buckets, you're thinking like a service desk professional, and ITIL stops being jargon and starts being useful.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: ITIL is shared best practice for IT services.
Incident: restore fast. Problem: fix the cause.
Change: improve safely. Request: provide.
Sort every contact into the right bucket.
Task: classify four scenarios with reasons.
slides.narration: Let's recap. ITIL is the shared best-practice framework for delivering IT services. The four ideas you'll use daily are: incidents, which you restore fast; problems, where you remove the root cause; changes, which you make safely; and service requests, which you fulfil. Your task: take the four scenarios on the page, label each as incident, problem, change, or service request, and write one sentence justifying each choice. That habit of classification will serve you for your whole career. See you next time.
